extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and advanced law students studying infringement and remedies
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding standards for determining infringement of different patent types (process, machine, manufacture, composition, design, improvement) and for choosing legal vs equitable remedies; includes doctrines like equivalents, product-of-machine, and procedural notes on jurisdiction and relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process patent — all essential steps rule
rubrics_metrics.description: A process is infringed only where every step claimed as essential is used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patentee's claimed essential steps must all be practiced for infringement (cases cited: Arnold v. Phelps, Hamerschlag v. Garrett). If an asserted essential step is omitted, there is no infringement. (Accompanying text contrasts variants where mode varies or timing differs.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Process patent — variation in mode does not necessarily avoid infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: A process may be infringed though its mode of use is varied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the infringer uses a different mode of applying the process, infringement can occur so long as the essential steps (or their substantial equivalents) are practiced (cases cited: Cary v. Wolff, Boneless Fish v. Chicago Mfg. Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Process patent — sequence/timing can be dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: A process consisting in doing certain acts at a certain stage of events is not infringed by doing the same acts at a different stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When sequence or stage is part of the claimed process, performing the acts at a different stage may avoid infringement (cases cited: Royer v. Chicago Mfg. Co., Roberto).

rubrics_metrics.name: Process patent — when both process and material are claimed
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a process and its material both enter into an invention there is no infringement unless both are used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the invention is defined as the combination of a process plus a particular material, an accused product/process must appropriate both elements to infringe (text note: see Goodyear Dental Vulcanite Co. v. Davis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine patent — structural-law (essence) test
rubrics_metrics.description: A machine is infringed by any other which embodies the same structural law; the mode operandi or structural law of the mechanism is the essence of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences in appearance, form, number/arrangement of parts, uses, or relative perfection are immaterial if the accused machine embodies the same structural law and performs the same service in the same way or substantially the same way (cases: Cantrell v. Wallick; Grier v. Castle). Mere colorable alterations or adroit substitutions of mechanical equivalents should not avoid infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine patent — focus on operative parts, not mere construction
rubrics_metrics.description: In assessing infringement of a machine, attention is to be directed to the parts which do the work, not to matters of construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze the functional/operative elements that perform the patented service. Structural differences that do not alter the functional/substantive operation are irrelevant (see Holly v. Yeigennes Mach. Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine patent — acts constituting infringement (making, using, selling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Making, using, or selling a patented machine are acts of infringement; manufacture alone is an infringement even though it is never used or sold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intent to put a machine to practical use may be inferred from its construction; sale of the machine likewise infringes. However sale/use of products MADE BY the machine does not violate the machine patent unless collusion exists between seller/user and infringing machine operator (see Butz Thermo Electric Regulator Co. v. Jacobs Electric Co.; Waterbury Brass Co. v. Miller).

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine patent — non-infringement where operation mode substantially different
rubrics_metrics.description: A machine whose mode of operation is substantially different does not infringe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the accused machine operates in a materially different manner (not merely different form), that difference can avoid infringement (cases: Schmidt v. Freese; Wyeth v. Stone).

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine patent — multifunction machines and single-use patents
rubrics_metrics.description: A machine capable of serving two uses, at the option of its user, is an infringement on the same device intended for one use only when employed for that intended use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a patented device is for a particular use, an accused machine that can perform multiple uses nevertheless infringes if it is used for the patented use (cases: Holbrook v. Small).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture (product) patent — essential-characteristics test
rubrics_metrics.description: A patented manufacture is infringed by making, using, or selling any manufacture which possesses the same essential characteristics, although in other qualities the inventions may be totally dissimilar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine the essential attributes by examining the article's effects, functions, and method of performing them; the method of producing the infringing article is immaterial (cases: Goodyear v. Railroad; Celluloid Mfg. Co. v. American Zylonite Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture patent — purchaser and product-of-machine rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a manufacture is in the market, purchasers are not obliged to find out whether it was made by a patented machine or process; the product cannot be reached except in the hands of one who is in some manner connected with the use of the patented machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sale/use of the product by an innocent purchaser is generally not a violation of a machine patent, absent collusion with the infringer. The patentee's remedy typically targets the maker/operator (see Boyd v. McAlpin; Goodyear cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture patent — material/equivalents rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of equivalents in a manufacture is an infringement; when a patent covers an article only when made of certain materials it is not infringed by the same article made of different materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patent claims a product generically, use of equivalent materials that produce the same essential characteristics infringes (Singer v. Walmsley). But where the claim is limited to particular materials, making the article of different materials can avoid infringement (Western & Wells Mfg. Co. v. Bosenatock).

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition-of-matter — identity-by-ingredients-and-result
rubrics_metrics.description: Two compositions are identical when they possess the same or equivalent ingredients, united together in the same manner to produce the same result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patented composition is infringed by another composition having the same or equivalent ingredients combined to produce the same properties, regardless of the manufacturing process (cases: Woodward v. Morrison; Holmes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition-of-matter — process-limited product claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a product is patented as the result of a certain process, it is infringed only when made by that process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patentee limited the claim to a product made by a specific process, an accused product made by a different process may avoid infringement (cases: Van Camp v. Maryland Pavement Co.; Cochrane v. Anilin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition-of-matter — substitution-of-elements doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent for a composition of matter is infringed if the new element does the same thing as the one for which it is substituted, though otherwise different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substituting an ingredient that performs the same cooperative function to produce the claimed properties can infringe (cases: Smith v. Murphy). Use of chemical equivalents can constitute infringement (Woodward v. Morrison).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design patent — ordinary-observer test
rubrics_metrics.description: Two designs are identical when they appear to be the same to the eye of an ordinary observer; designs are infringed if resemblance is such as to deceive an ordinary observer and induce purchase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design-patent infringement is judged by visual similarity to ordinary purchasers, not necessarily an expert; copying a part of a design covered by the patent can infringe; differing trade names do not avoid infringement (cases: Miller v. Smith; Dittmar v. Rix; Dryfoos v. Friedman).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement patent — measure and infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: An improvement is measured by the specific change that renders operation more advantageous; an improvement patent is infringed by every other change which is substantially the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the improved feature before and after the improvement; infringement requires appropriation of the essential attributes of that specific change. An improvement in an art is infringed by practicing the art in the peculiar manner discovered by the improver, but not by practicing it in a different manner that yields the same result (see §§ 210-218 cross-references; Robertson v. Blake).

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of equivalents / disallowing colorable variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere colorable alterations or adroit evasions by substituting mechanical or chemical equivalents should not protect an infringer; use of equivalents can constitute infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts look to whether substituted parts or ingredients perform substantially the same function in substantially the same way to produce the same result; if so, they may be treated as equivalents (cases: Wheeler v. Clipper Mower & Reaper Co.; Woodward v. Morrison).

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint ownership and consent liability
rubrics_metrics.description: Where one of several co-owners of an infringing machine operates it with the consent of the others, the act is theirs as well and all are infringers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Co-owners who permit operation of an infringing machine can be held liable as joint infringers (see Woodworth v. Edwards).

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-of-machine — limits on reaching downstream sellers/users
rubrics_metrics.description: The sale, use, or sale of manufactured products of a patented machine does not violate the patent unless the user or seller are in collusion with the infringing operator of the machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patentee generally cannot reach innocent downstream purchasers; liability attaches when there is collusion or when the purchaser is connected with the infringing manufacture (see Boyd v. McAlpin; related discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies — law (damages) vs equity (injunction, discovery, accounting)
rubrics_metrics.description: An action at law yields damages for past infringements; equity provides injunctions, discovery, accounting, and other relief to prevent continuing or secret infringements and to secure full protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages alone are often inadequate for continuing or secret wrongs; courts of equity may enjoin future infringement, compel disclosure of extent/character of infringement, and grant an account. Choice of remedy depends on nature of injury and available relief (historical statutory background and cases cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural/jurisdictional rules relevant to remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurisdiction over patent cases is vested exclusively in the Federal courts; no previous notice is needed to sue; arbitration clauses can be binding; some state claims (e.g., against counties) may require pre-suit presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal courts have both legal and equitable jurisdiction in patent cases (statutory evolution). Plaintiffs need not give prior notice before suing; however contractual arbitration requirements or special local pre-suit statutory requirements may affect procedure (cases: Ames v. Howard; Perkins v. United States Electric Light Co.; May v. Buchanan Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity practice — courts may refuse jury trial in complex patent matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts of equity historically and presently may assume control over patent causes and often treat them as unfit for jury trials, deciding complex patent issues by judge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chancery practice and later equity jurisdiction permitted hearings without jury where technical/complicated questions made jury trial unsuitable; modern courts may similarly prefer non-jury resolution for intricate patent questions (cases and commentary: Harmer v. Plane; Bovin v. Hitchcock; Lord Selborne in Patent Marine Inventions Co. v. Chadburn).
